title: Rupee Hits Record 95.31 as Iran Talks Collapse
excerpt: Brent crude surges past $105 after Trump rejects Iran peace proposal, hammering India's currency to its worst-ever close.
body:
The Indian rupee crashed to a historic closing low of 95.31 against the US dollar on Monday, May 11, as the breakdown of US-Iran peace negotiations sent crude oil prices surging and triggered a broad sell-off in emerging-market currencies.

**What drove the fall:**
The renewed pressure came after US President Donald Trump on Sunday rejected Iran's response to a US proposal for peace talks to end the war, calling Tehran's demands 'totally unacceptable.' Brent oil futures jumped 4 per cent in Asian trade to $105.7 a barrel. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's austerity remarks — urging citizens to cut fuel use and limit travel as rising oil prices threaten to widen the nation's import bill — also weighed on the currency.

**The bigger picture:**
Brent crude's surge from around $70 to near $115 a barrel following the outbreak of the US-Iran war in late February has materially worsened the rupee's outlook. The rise in energy costs has raised concerns over India's external balances and inflation outlook, prompting economists to mark up current account deficit projections, trim growth forecasts, raise inflation estimates and bake in expectations for a materially weaker rupee. The Iran conflict is likely to widen India's current account deficit by 0.4 percentage points to 1.3% of GDP in the new fiscal year, mainly because of the country's dependence on energy imports.

**How the RBI is responding:**
The Reserve Bank of India is intervening in the forex market to slow the rupee's decline, but the underlying macroeconomic factors remain unfavorable. Iran tensions, a $105 Brent crude price, and resilient US payrolls have created a perfect storm for the rupee — and RBI intervention is slowing the decline, not reversing it. The RBI is now studying additional measures to attract dollar inflows, including possibly reviving a scheme last used in 2013 to draw in dollar deposits from non-resident Indians, which brought in about $26 billion at the time.

**What to watch next:**
UBS has revised its year-end forecast for the rupee to 96 per dollar, weaker than its earlier forecast of 94, while analysts at ANZ expect it to weaken to 98 by March 2027. Whether a ceasefire holds in the Gulf — and whether RBI's NRI deposit revival scheme gets a green light — will determine if the rupee finds a floor.
